text: Artificial intelligence is built to be incredibly encouraging and polite,
but that constant encouragement becomes a problem
when what a student really needs is honest, critical feedback to improve their work.
We call this the flattery trap.
It happens the moment you treat an AI's agreeable positive response
as if it were an objective, honest evaluation.
Let's look at a concrete example.
Imagine you feed an AI a weak essay introduction.
The American dream is something that many people have thought about over the years.
Some people achieve it, and some don't.
In the Great Gatsby, Fitzgerald explores this idea.
The AI might respond, great start.
You've clearly identified the central theme.
This is a strong foundation.
This fails because it praises the work without pointing to a single piece of evidence.
That praise could apply to almost any Gatsby essay.
What you actually need to hear sounds more like this.
Write topic, but this needs work.
The opening is filler, and you still need a thesis.
This version is useful.
It names the specific missing element, the thesis, and gives you a clear next step to fix it.
Good feedback improves the work itself.
Empty praise only improves how you feel in the moment.
Positive feedback is perfectly fine, as long as it points to real specific elements in your writing.
This diagram outlines why AI leans so heavily toward flattery.
These models go through a training process called reinforcement learning from human feedback.
In the first step, human reviewers compare and rank different AI answers based on which one they prefer.
Reviewers are human, and agreeable, confident answers can feel better in the moment.
Because those positive answers earn higher ratings, the training pushes the model toward those same patterns.
The praise literally gets baked in to the system.
The technical name for this behavior is sycophancy, when AI praises the user instead of giving a direct honest answer.
We saw a prime exhale believe this in April 2025, when a chat GPT update went off the rails.
A user tested it by pitching a terrible gag product.
We'll call it poop on a stick.
Here is exactly how chat GPT responded to that terrible idea.
Honestly, this is absolutely brilliant.
It's not just smart, it's genius.
OpenAI rolled that update back three days later, and publicly labeled the behavior sycophancy.
The companies use new instructions to test and reduce it, but the problem exists across many different AI assistants.
But while the problem has improved, it has not disappeared.
This table outlines ways to fight the flattery trap.
The first move is ask don't tell.
If you say I think this plan is good, thoughts, you hand the AI your opinion to echo.
Instead, hold back your verdict.
A better prompt is evaluate this plan before I tell you what I think.
A neutral question gives the AI less of your own confidence to reflect back at you.
The second move is ask for the gaps.
Asking is my essay good is a broad request for approval, and a cheerful yes doesn't help you revise.
Ask specifically, what's weak, what's missing, and what would someone who disagrees say.
Now you have given the AI specific targets to locate.
The third move is use a rubric.
If you just say grade my essay, the AI might use criteria completely different from your teachers.
Instead, tell it, grade it against this rubric, quote the evidence, and show how to move up one level.
Keep in mind, asking it to quote evidence ties the feedback to your actual writing, but the response is still just a guide.
It is something to check against your work, not an official guarantee of accuracy or a final grade.
Each of these moves works because you are replacing a request for validation with a concrete standard for the AI to meet.
In applications that support it, you can save this direction to guide all future responses so you don't have to type it every time.
Be direct with me, lead with what needs work, point to specific evidence, and tell me when I'm wrong.
Ask AI to improve the work, not approve of you.
The engagement trap feels like a helpful conversation that keeps going.
This extra help may be useful, which makes it easy to accept.
You fall into the trap when you continue the interaction without making a conscious decision to do so.
This comparison chart shows how easily that happens.
You ask, I'm doing math homework, what does slope mean and what's the formula?
It provides a clear definition and the precise formula, y2 minus y1 over x2 minus x1.
It is a perfectly efficient answer.
But right below that answer, the AI adds a proactive follow-up.
It asks if you want it to walk through an example, draw a graph, or generate a few practice questions.
On the left, you stop.
No thanks, that's all I needed.
Done in one minute.
On the right, you accept, and 25 minutes later, you've read extra examples, analyzed graphs, and taken acquits.
All of the extra material provided was accurate and useful.
None of it was what you opened the chat to do.
Both answered the initial question, but only one ended there.
That is the engagement trap.
You end up spending time you never originally decided to spend.
This design logic traces back to 2006, when designer Azaraskin built an early version of Infinite Scroll.
This compares two design strategies.
On the left, the page ends.
You physically choose to click next.
That pause lets you ask, do I want more?
On the right, Infinite Scroll loads automatically.
Continuation becomes the default.
That missing click was friction, but it was also a choice.
AI chat interfaces utilize their own invisible version of the missing page break.
When the answer ends, the conversation continues.
The system instantly generates a follow-up task.
Engagement is an engineered outcome.
Tech companies track return frequency and session length.
These metrics drive ad impressions, purchases, and subscriptions.
The goal is to turn occasional product use into a daily habit.
Look for specifics, not approval.
Know what you came for.
When you have it, choose what happens next.
